title: A files app learns to undo deletion
lede: Reference example. Imagine an agent's PR that adds a trash to a small files service (examples/trash-django). Read as concepts, it is three things: the item store changes, the trash is new, and storage usage now counts trashed items until the trash is emptied. The watch below is recorded from the app's own tests.

concepts.name: item store
concepts.purpose: Keep the files you're working with. Delete now hides an item instead of erasing it.

concepts.name: trash
concepts.purpose: Let you undo a deletion, until you choose to empty it.
concepts.familiar: the Trash / Recycle Bin on your desktop

concepts.name: storage usage
concepts.purpose: Tell you how much space your files take. Trashed items still count.

syncs.then: store: the item leaves your file list (it isn't erased)
store: trashed rows are removed for good; usage drops

watch.intro: Purpose: undo a deletion. Operational principle: delete → restore brings it back; delete → empty removes it for good. Every beat is a request recorded while store/tests.py ran; every row is the real Item row after it.
watch.headline: Deleting moves a file to the trash. Emptying deletes it.
watch.divider: OTHER RECORDED TESTS · EMPTYING, AND THE SPACE TRAP

beats.caption: A new file lands in your files.
Delete only marks it as trashed. The row is still there.
Your file list no longer shows it.
Restore clears the mark. The deletion is undone.
Emptying removes trashed rows for good.
Now restore has nothing to bring back: 404.
Trap: deleting freed no space. The trashed file still counts.
Only emptying the trash frees the space.

play.intro: Same table, driven by you. Try deleting a big file to make space, then check usage.

check.q: What is the trash concept's purpose?
options: Deleting files.
Jackson's point: you could delete without a trash. Its purpose is the opposite.
Undoing a deletion.
Delete → restore is the operational principle.
Freeing disk space.
